debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: You aren't asking for too much. You are simply observing a break in the proximity-seeking behaviors that humans rely on to feel secure in a bond. When someone is inconsistently available, it triggers an alarm.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: [Basis: John Bowlby, Attachment and Loss, Vol 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_and_Loss)

debate.speaker: The Social Psychologist
debate.text: That assumes the person is acting from a consistent internal state. I see the 'date' as a performance where they play the lover, but the 'between-dates' is when they step off-stage, retreating into their private, unperformed self.
debate.author: Erving Goffman
debate.book: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
debate.basis: [Basis: Erving Goffman, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, Chapter 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Presentation_of_Self_in_Everyday_Life)

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: But you are torturing yourself with the story of their silence. What is the observable fact? They show up when present. The rest is just your judgment that their silence implies a lack of care.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: It isn't just judgment. When a secure base is unpredictable, it triggers real biological anxiety. Ignoring that doesn't make it go away; it leaves you tethered to a phantom, waiting for a signal that may never come.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: [Basis: John Bowlby, Attachment and Loss, Vol 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_and_Loss)

debate.speaker: The Social Psychologist
debate.text: Precisely. The user is trying to find a coherent script where none exists. The 'date' character and the 'texting' character might not be the same person's intended design, leading to this confusion.
debate.author: Erving Goffman
debate.book: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
debate.basis: [Basis: Erving Goffman, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, Chapter 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Presentation_of_Self_in_Everyday_Life)

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: I concede that point. If the inconsistency creates ongoing suffering, the user has a right to demand a clearer role, even if the other person is merely playing a part in their own life.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: Exactly. If they are avoidant, they might need space to regulate, but you need consistency to attach. It is a fundamental friction in needs, not a failing on your part. You have to ask if this friction is sustainable.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: [Basis: John Bowlby, Attachment and Loss, Vol 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_and_Loss)

debate.speaker: The Social Psychologist
debate.text: Wait, let’s be careful. Could the silence be a lack of interest, or is it just how they manage their 'backstage' privacy? We are labeling them without enough evidence of their intent.
debate.author: Erving Goffman
debate.book: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
debate.basis: [Basis: Erving Goffman, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, Chapter 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Presentation_of_Self_in_Everyday_Life)

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: Then the choice is clear. The user should act on the observable fact—the silence is real—and see if communicating that discomfort yields a change or merely reveals a fixed boundary that cannot be crossed.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

output.clearer: The debate clarified that the user's distress may not stem from being 'too demanding' but from a mismatch between their need for consistency and the partner's compartmentalized communication style.
